newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Looming supply to depress Singapore home prices.
newsitem.headline: Looming supply to depress Singapore home prices.

text.p: Singapore home prices are likely to remain depressed over the next 12 months with a growing stock of unsold units building up, property analysts said on Thursday.
They said a price correction of between 10-15 percent over the next year looked likely as developers face the prospect of either keeping their housing stock or cutting prices.

"Developers have been trying to hold on to their prices. A few of them are also trying to postpone the launch of their projects into next year to ease the supply situation," said Ng Yaw Tong, property analyst with GK Goh Securities.
But it looks like time is running against developers as supply continues to build up.
About 22,700 new homes are scheduled to be launched from the third quarter of 1997 to 1998, real estate consultants Edmund Tie & Co (ET&Co) said in their latest quarter report.
Annual demand is expected to be sharply. Analysts expect take-up rates for new homes to be abount 6,000 units this year against 9,000 in the past few years.
Demand is shrinking because of falling affordibility and doubts over whether property prices will hold up.

"A lot of people are just waiting for lower prices. We are not talking about satisfying a need in Singapore as 90 percent of the population are home owners. We are talking about satisfying aspirations," said Ong Choon Fah, executive director at ET&Co.
Singapore's highly successful public housing programme has meant homes for the bulk of the population and growing affluence has led many to aspire to own private homes, driving up prices.
But buyers are finding its harder with rising prices coupled with government moves in May 1996 to tighten credit in a bid to curb property asset inflation.
"Affordability has been reduced. Buyers have to put down 20 percent in cash up front and many find it hard to come up with the cash," said Lim Chung Chun of ING Barings.

A slew of recent events has also dampened buying, including a much publicised letter from the chairman of the Real Estate Developers of Singapore (REDAS), asking the government to slow land sales because the market was "sick".
The Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) showed that stock of unsold new homes stood at 15,527 at the end of June, up 18 percent from the end of March.

"Activity was actually picking up in the second quarter in terms of number of transactions. But after the REDAS publicity, activity has slowed considerably. There is a lot of cash and interest to buy out there -- we still get calls asking us if
there are any bargains", said Ong.
"It is a waiting gaming between developers and buyers to see who blinks first. This time round, it looks like buyers are digging in their heels a bit," she said.
Analysts said developers looked likely to lose out this time as cash flow problem loom if they do not sell.

"Developers are worried because there will be a cash flow problem son. Many of them have paid high prices for their land and land cost constitue about 70 percent of total cost of a development," said one consultant who declined to be named.
Analysts said the Singapore property market was unlikely to face a meltdown similar to that in Thailand, where developers defaulted on loans, leaving banks with bad property assets.

"I don't expect a big adverse impact on the financial system. But we are looking at potential capital loss for home owners and poor earnings for property developers. Banks earnings will also be affected because a slowdown in home loans," Lim said.
